textbookText: Discuss the following questions: i. Why did early scientists find the study of life so intriguing, leading to the creation of biology? ii. What makes biology important in our daily lives? iii. How has our knowledge of living things influenced fields like medicine and agriculture? iv. How does biology contribute to solving global challenges? v. Can we understand biology without knowledge of other branches of science?

We are accompanied by plenty of living creatures found on the earth. Many of them are harmless and useful while some are harmful. There is a science that studies all forms of such lives known as biology (Greek: ‘bios’ – life, ‘logos’ - knowledge). Thus, it is also known as life science.

The major contributions in the development of biology were made by Hippocrates (460-320 BC), Aristotle (384 - 322 BC), Theophrastus (370 - 285 BC), Robert Hooke (1635 - 1703 AD), Carolus Linnaeus (1707 - 1778 AD), Charles Darwin (1809 - 1882 AD), Gregor John Mendel (1822 - 1884 AD) and many other biologists.

Do you know? • The term 'Biology' was coined by Lamarck and Treviranus (1802). • The father of biology is Aristotle. • The father of zoology is Aristotle. • The father of botany is Theophrastus. • The father of medicine is Hippocrates.
The three main branches of biology which deal with the different aspects of living science are:
1. Botany (Greek: 'botanē' = herbs, ‘logos’ - knowledge/study) - It is the branch of biology that deals with the study of plants.
2. Zoology (Greek: 'zōion' = animal, ‘logos’ - knowledge/study) - It is the branch of biology that studies about animals.
3. Microbiology (Greek ‘mikros’ - small or slight, ‘logos’ - knowledge/study) – It is the branch of biology that studies tiny living creatures that cannot be observed by our naked eyes.
